City (pop., 2024: 1,050,153) on a plateau in the Judaean Mountains, in the Southern Levant between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea. One of the oldest cities in the world, it is holy to the three [[Abrahamic religions]]: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

The City of David shows first signs of settlement in the 4th millennium BC, in the form of encampments of nomadic shepherds. Egyptian tablets of the 14th century BC name the city Urusalim, probably meaning "foundation of [the god] Shalem." Radiocarbon dating of 103 samples shows Iron Age settlement in the 12th–10th centuries BC and growth until the Babylonian destruction in 586 BC. According to the Hebrew Bible, King David made it the capital of the United Kingdom of Israel and his son Solomon commissioned the First Temple. Jerusalem has been destroyed at least twice, besieged 23 times, captured and recaptured 44 times, and attacked 52 times. The walls that define the Old City were rebuilt in 1538 under [[Suleiman the Magnificent]]. The Old City became a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1981.

Despite covering only 0.9 km², the Old City contains the [[Temple Mount]], with the Western Wall, Dome of the Rock, and Al-Aqsa Mosque, and the [[Church of the Holy Sepulchre]]. Christians associate the city with the crucifixion and resurrection of Jesus. In Islam it is the third-holiest city, after Mecca and Medina, and was the first direction of Muslim prayer.

Israel occupied East Jerusalem from Jordan in 1967 following the [[Six-Day War]] and annexed it. The 1980 Jerusalem Law calls the city Israel's undivided capital, and the Knesset and Supreme Court sit there. Neither Israel's nor Palestine's claim to the city as capital is widely recognized internationally, and its status remains a core issue in the [[Israeli–Palestinian conflict]].

Jewish preacher and religious leader active in the Roman province of Judaea in the 1st century, and the central figure of [[Christianity]]. Most branches of Christianity consider him the incarnation of God the Son and the awaited [[Messiah]].

Accounts of his life appear chiefly in the four canonical Gospels of the [[New Testament]]. Academic research since the Enlightenment has produced varied views on their historical reliability, but virtually all modern scholars of antiquity agree that he existed historically. According to Christian tradition, he was baptized by [[John the Baptist]], fasted 40 days and nights in the Judean wilderness, and then began a public ministry as an itinerant teacher. He debated Pharisees and Sadducees over how best to follow God, engaged in healings, taught in parables, and appointed 12 apostles.

The New Testament accounts state that he was arrested in Jerusalem, tried by the Sanhedrin, and crucified on the order of [[Pontius Pilate]], the Roman prefect of Judaea. Christians believe he rose from the dead on the third day, a belief that became the foundation of the early Church. Christian theology holds that he was born of the virgin Mary, performed miracles, died as a sacrifice for atonement for sin, ascended into Heaven, and will return to judge the living and the dead. Many branches regard him as the second person of the [[Trinity]].

His birth in Bethlehem is celebrated generally on 25 December as [[Christmas]], and his resurrection on [[Easter]] Sunday. Mainstream Judaism rejects the belief that he was the messiah or divine. Islam honors him as a prophet and messiah sent to the Israelites, but not as God or the son of God, and most Muslims hold that he was not crucified.

Decorative items worn for personal adornment, such as brooches, rings, necklaces, earrings, pendants, bracelets, and cufflinks. The American spelling is *jewelry*. The word derives from *jewel*, which entered English from Old French *jouel* and ultimately from Latin *jocale*, meaning "plaything."

From a Western perspective the term is restricted to durable ornaments. For many centuries gold and silver, often combined with [[Gemstone|gemstones]], have been the standard materials, while [[Amber|amber]], [[Coral|coral]], glass, shells, wood, bone, ivory, clay, and enamel are also used. Platinum alloys range from 900 (90% pure) to 950 (95% pure), and the silver used is usually sterling silver, 92.5% fine. Makers employ forging, casting, soldering or welding, cutting, carving, and "cold-joining" with adhesives, staples, and rivets. Beads, including the small seed beads used in woven styles, are common, and beadwork is prominent in many African and indigenous North American cultures.

Jewellery is among the oldest types of archaeological artefact, and perforated shell beads are cited as early evidence of personal decoration. Its uses include fixing clothing or hair in place, marking social status (as with wedding rings and chains of office), signifying ethnic, religious, or social affiliation (as with the Christian crucifix or the Jewish Star of David), providing talismanic protection through amulets, artistic display, and carrying personal meaning such as love, mourning, or luck. Many items, such as brooches and buckles, began as purely functional objects and became decorative. Some cultures store wedding dowries as jewellery, and it has served as currency or a trade good.

[[Diamond|Diamonds]] were first mined in [[India]]. In 2005 Australia, Botswana, Russia, and Canada ranked among the primary sources of gemstone diamond production.

German composer and musician of the late Baroque period.

Bach is known for his prolific output across many instruments and forms: the orchestral [[Brandenburg Concertos|*Brandenburg Concertos*]]; the *Cello Suites* and the Sonatas and Partitas for solo violin; keyboard works such as the *Goldberg Variations* and [[The Well-Tempered Clavier|*The Well-Tempered Clavier*]]; organ works including the Toccata and Fugue in D minor; and choral works such as the *St. Matthew Passion* and the [[Mass in B minor|*Mass in B minor*]]. His mastery of [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]] is heard in *The Musical Offering* and *The Art of Fugue*, and many of his works use techniques such as canon and [[Fugue|fugue]].

Born in Eisenach, the youngest child of the town musician Johann Ambrosius Bach, he was orphaned at age 10 and lived for five years with his eldest brother, Johann Christoph, before continuing his education in Lüneburg. From 1703 he worked as a church musician in [[Thuringia]], at Arnstadt and Mühlhausen. By 1723 he was Thomaskantor, responsible for music in four Lutheran city churches and for the St. Thomas School in [[Leipzig]]. There he composed annual cycles of church cantatas, wrote for the university's Collegium Musicum, and began publishing his keyboard music in 1726. In 1736 Augustus III of Poland named him court composer of the Elector of Saxony. Four of his twenty children, Wilhelm Friedemann, Carl Philipp Emanuel, Johann Christoph Friedrich, and Johann Christian, became composers.

He blended German traditions with rhythms, forms, and textures from Italy and France, and wrote hundreds of cantatas, Passions, oratorios, motets, concertos, and suites. Few works were printed in his lifetime, and he was known mainly as an organist. [[Felix Mendelssohn]] precipitated the Bach Revival with a performance of the *St. Matthew Passion* in 1829.

German inventor and craftsman who created the movable-type printing press in Europe.

Born in Mainz into a patrician family, he trained as a goldsmith, metallurgist, and gem cutter. A letter of March 1434 places him in [[Strasbourg]], where he appears to have been enrolled in the militia as a goldsmith, and in 1437 he was teaching a wealthy tradesman to polish gems. Movable type was already in use in East Asia, but his methods allowed a much faster rate of printing.

His contributions include a process for mass-producing movable type, adjustable molds, oil-based [[Ink|ink]], and a wooden [[Printing press|printing press]] modeled on the agricultural screw presses of the period. His method of making type is traditionally held to have used a hand mould and a type-metal [[Alloy|alloy]] of lead, tin, and [[Antimony|antimony]], which melted at a relatively low temperature, cast well, and produced durable type. By about 1450 he had established a printing workshop in Mainz. His major work, the [[Gutenberg Bible]] (c. 1455), was the first printed version of the Bible and has been acclaimed for its aesthetic and technical quality. Financial difficulties followed: a lawsuit from the investor Johann Fust led to the loss of his press and equipment in 1456.

The printing press later spread across the world and led to an information revolution and the mass spread of literature in Europe, with a profound effect on the [[Renaissance]], the [[Reformation]], and humanist movements. To mark the 500th anniversary of his birth, the Gutenberg Museum was founded in Mainz in 1900. In 1997 Time Life picked his invention as the most important of the second millennium.

English philosopher and physician, among the most influential thinkers of the Enlightenment and commonly called the "father of [[Liberalism|liberalism]]."

His major works, all of 1689–90, are *A Letter Concerning Toleration*, *Two Treatises of Government*, and *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding*. The *Letter* contends that religion is a matter for the individual and that churches are voluntary associations, ruling out religious coercion and uniformity. The *Two Treatises* argue for government based on the consent of the governed and for a right to revolt against tyranny. They are believed to have influenced the language [[Thomas Jefferson]] chose for the 1776 Declaration of Independence.

In the *Essay*, Locke argued that the mind at birth is a blank slate, or *tabula rasa*, and that knowledge comes only from experience through sense perception, a position known as [[Empiricism|empiricism]] and associated with the tradition of [[Francis Bacon]]. He is also credited with describing private property as a natural right arising when a person mixes labor with nature.

Born in Wrington, Somerset, to Puritan parents, he attended Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, where he spent 15 years as student and tutor and pursued medicine. From 1666 he was an associate of Lord Shaftesbury and held government posts through him. He lived in exile in the [[Netherlands]] in 1683–85, returned in 1689 after the [[Glorious Revolution]], and later served as a Commissioner of Trade and Plantations.

His ties to [[Slavery|slavery]] remain debated: he was a shareholder in the Royal Company of Adventures Trading to Africa, which traded in slaves, and was involved in the Carolina proprietorship, which permitted slavery. Scholars continue to discuss the contradiction with his theory of natural liberty.

Soviet politician and revolutionary who led the [[Soviet Union]] from the late 1920s until 1953.

Born Ioseb Jughashvili into a poor Georgian family in Gori, he left a Tiflis seminary in 1899 and became a Marxist revolutionary. Active in the Caucasus, he raised funds for the Bolshevik faction through robberies and other crimes and was repeatedly arrested and exiled to Siberia. After the [[October Revolution]] of 1917 he joined the Politburo. Following the death of [[Vladimir Lenin]] in 1924, he used his post as General Secretary of the Communist Party (1922–52) to outmaneuver rivals and by the 1930s was the de facto dictator.

His policy of "Socialism in One Country" and five-year plans from 1928 brought rapid collectivization of agriculture and industrialization under a centralized command economy. State policy contributed to a major famine in 1930–33, most severe in Ukraine and Kazakhstan. During the [[Great Purge]] of 1936–39, at least 700,000 people were executed and over a million imprisoned in the Gulag system.

In 1939 his government signed a non-aggression pact with [[Nazi Germany]], leading to the joint invasion of Poland and the Soviet annexation of the Baltic states. After Germany invaded in 1941, the Red Army repelled Axis forces and captured Berlin in 1945. The Soviets helped establish aligned governments in Central and Eastern Europe, China, and North Korea, forming the [[Eastern Bloc]], and the start of the [[Cold War]] with the United States followed.

After his death [[Nikita Khrushchev]] denounced him and began de-Stalinization. Within the international Marxist–Leninist movement he was the subject of a pervasive personality cult. He retains popularity in Russia as a victorious wartime leader, while his regime has been widely condemned for mass repression, ethnic cleansing, and the deaths of millions.

Production and distribution of reports on events, facts, ideas, and people that constitute the "[[News|news]] of the day," with a commitment to accuracy and verification. The word applies to the occupation (professional or not), the methods of gathering information, and the organizing literary styles.

Its role varies across countries. In some nations news media are controlled by the government and lack independence; in others they operate as independent private enterprises. Legal frameworks also differ, particularly regarding [[Freedom of speech|freedom of speech]], freedom of the press, slander, and libel. Journalism is said to act as a "fourth estate," a watchdog on government.

In the United States, many credible news organizations are incorporated, have editorial boards, and keep separate editorial and advertising departments. Many belong to professional bodies such as the Society of Professional Journalists, whose ethics emphasize seeking truth, minimizing harm, acting independently, and being accountable. Newspapers separate fact from opinion by section, with opinion pieces written by columnists or placed in an op-ed section. Whether ethics require journalists to be objective and neutral is widely debated. Critics cite studies finding ideological skew in major outlets, and one survey figure put U.S. trust in mass media at 28% in 2025.

Forms include access, advocacy, broadcast, business, citizen, data, and drone journalism.

The spread of the [[Internet|internet]] and [[Smartphone|smartphones]] since the early 21st century has changed how audiences obtain news, with growing use of mobile devices and digital platforms rather than print or television. Print newspapers have declined or disappeared in some regions, and print revenues have fallen faster than digital income has grown, leaving news organizations struggling to monetize digital content.

Abrahamic, monotheistic, ethnic religion comprising the spiritual, cultural, and legal traditions of the [[Jews|Jewish people]]. Religious Jews regard it as their means of observing the Mosaic covenant, believed to have been established between God and the Jewish people. It is considered one of the earliest monotheistic religions.

Its core texts are the [[Torah]] ("Teaching"), the Nevi'im ("Prophets"), and the Ketuvim ("Writings"), which together form the [[Hebrew Bible]], also called the Tanakh. The Oral Torah comprises the Mishnah and the [[Talmud]], Midrashim, [[Halakha]] (Jewish law), Aggadah, and later rabbinic commentary. Rabbinic Judaism holds that God revealed commandments to Moses on Mount Sinai in both written and oral form.

The largest movements are [[Orthodox Judaism]], [[Conservative Judaism]], and [[Reform Judaism]]. They differ in their approaches to Halakha, rabbinic authority, and rabbinic literature, and in the significance they give to the State of Israel. Orthodox Judaism maintains that the Torah and Halakha are divine, eternal, and unalterable. Conservative Judaism generally takes a more traditionalist line than Reform, whose typical position treats Halakha as general guidelines. Authority is vested not in any one person or body but in the texts and in the rabbis and scholars who interpret them.

The term derives from Latin *Iudaismus*, from Greek *Ioudaismos*, first attested in 2 Maccabees in the 2nd century BC, and ultimately from the Hebrew *Yehudah* (Judah). Scholars debate the religion's origins: many critical historians describe an evolution from Yahwism, the ancient Israelite worship of Yahweh in the Iron Age, while others argue for an earlier distinct covenant. Jewishness may pass by matrilineal descent or conversion, so secular individuals may still belong to the people. Judaism strongly influenced Christianity and Islam. In 2025 the world Jewish population was estimated at 14.8 million.

Roman general, statesman, and author, dictator of the [[Roman Republic]] almost continuously from 49 BC until his assassination in 44 BC.

Born into the patrician gens Julia, which claimed descent from Venus, Caesar rose through factional politics. In 60 BC he formed the First Triumvirate, an informal alliance with Crassus and [[Pompey]] that dominated Roman politics for several years and was opposed by many senators, including Cato the Younger. As proconsul of Gaul from 58 BC he conducted the [[Gallic Wars]], completed by 51 BC, which greatly expanded Roman territory. During them he invaded Britain and built a bridge across the Rhine.

When the Senate ordered him to give up his command, Caesar crossed the Rubicon in early January 49 BC and marched on Rome, beginning a civil war that he won, leaving him in near-unchallenged power by 45 BC. After pardoning many enemies he carried out reforms and public works. He created the [[Julian calendar]] to replace the republican lunisolar calendar, reduced the grain dole, settled veterans in new overseas colonies, greatly increased the size of the Senate, and extended citizenship to communities in Spain and what is now northern Italy.

In early 44 BC he was proclaimed "dictator in perpetuity." Fearing his power and the possibility that he would make himself king, a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius assassinated him on the Ides of March, 44 BC. His great-nephew and adoptive heir Octavian, later [[Augustus]], eventually transformed the Republic into the [[Roman Empire]].

Much of his life is known from his own campaign accounts, the letters and speeches of [[Cicero]], and the biographies of Suetonius and Plutarch. His cognomen became a synonym for emperor, giving rise to *Kaiser* and *Tsar*.
